Man

This is making an edit to an existing design, when for the scope (adding new IPCs to openbmc) it really needs its own design doc, specifically the requirements and alternatives considered sections need filled out that justify fuse, and talk through the full usage of FUSE in the lifecycle of openbmc.

My "default" implementation for a PLDM file transfer feature I would expect to be:
1. Create a dbus interface that allows requesting a file
2. Implement DBus interface in pldm
3. Implement Dbus interface in bmcweb to host the redfish interface (ideally sharing the code we already use for existing dump types)

I'd like to see at least of a minimum analysis of why that path isn't possible/nonperformant/unmaintainable documented.


I really think FUSE would be an interesting addition from a diagnostics perspective, but in terms of hosting an API that the rest of the system can use, we've found the fileystem to be lacking in its ability to handle errors, pass concurrent requests, model complex systems, or handle non-blocking IO in a single threaded daemon.  If we have those concerns addressed, ideally that would show up in the new design under impacts, and the design section would call out how those things are managed.

FWIW, firmware updates just moved its mechanism AWAY from the filesystem because of these problems, so proposing we implement something that looks very much like the old firmware update system that we just moved away from should probably be addressed head on in the design doc as well.
Thanks for your feedback. We will feedback after the internal discussion.

After reconsideration the effects and looking at new FW update design, we decided to not involve libfuse, but propose a common File.Object D-Bus interface to allow apps to interact with files published by pldmd. Thanks for your feedbacks and information. Can you please help give your opinions about our update to the PS? The PS will now focus on PLDM implementation only, more about the flow to collect those files via Redfish will be in a separate patch after this is direction is approved.
Resolved this as the design has been updated to leverage a file D-Bus interface.
This is not the documentation for redfish.  This is the documentation for PLDM.

Remove.  Task service versus normal call is an implementation detail that already exists in bmcweb.  We're not going to redesign TaskService as part of this design.

How does FUSE communicate to bmcweb?  bmcweb specifically can't do blocking io calls today without blocking other connections (see COMMON_ERRORS.md), of which a filesystem read would be a blocking call to FUSE.

If you plan to implement a solution to this (threads, uring, etc) that really should be discussed in a patchset.
Removed libfuse involvement from the design.

According to Table 9 DfOpen Command Format (Section 9.2.5 DSP0242 v1.0.0). `DfOpenAttribute` field in DfOpen command has `DfOpenReadWrite` bitfield not supporting `Write` so I mentioned that it's not supported. Should I remove the sentence to save it for future?

Why is this a concern? This is how async applications are implemented anyway (or via `io_uring`).
Acknowledged. I will address this after my concerns about socketpair are cleared.

Agree with arj's statement here, this can be implemented using async IO, where we open the socket in NONBLOCKING mode, and let the application be waiting on eventloop and execute the transfer only when ever the data becomes available.

But I see some problems with socket, where  pldmd has to rely on the client to start reading the data off, or the kernel buffer will overflow. pldmd and the client app has to cover how long to wait for the socket's readiness and error handling. While with memfd, when it's returned from the D-Bus method to the client, it's ready for the client to read. Do you think I should update to mention these in the comparison?

> or the kernel buffer will overflow.

What do you mean by this? If the socket buffer is full the socket is not write-ready and so pldmd won't write to it. Overflows are prevented this way. Once a read has been performed the socket buffer is (partially) drained and so becomes write-ready, allowing pldmd to write more data. pldmd continues to read the file from the device until the data transfer is complete or the client application closes its socket.

What we're proposing is that pldmd act like a proxy. That's not an unusual thing to do.
Blocking concerns are invalid, removed.

Does DfOpen need to be called always or will the file be kept open by file host?

File host can unilaterally close the file fd if there's no DfHeartbeat or DfRead coming from file client within the NegotiatedInterval (see DSP0242 v1.0.0 Section 9.6 DfHeartbeat Command for definition).

Moreover, file host can provide different fds for multiple sessions open simultaneously to the file. Therefore, there's no use to preserve one single fd always open for one file object (can be achieved by periodically sending DfHeartbeat to File Host). Each D-Bus call will open a session of its own and manipulate its own fd.
Agree, But is dfHeartbeat is accounted else where for SerialFIFO (Streaming) kind of file? This flow covers only regular files?

No, this design covers both file types.

For SerialFIFO types, the spec says:

> This method (DfHeartbeat) typically is used to inform the File Client when a SerialTxFIFO file is approaching capacity and needs a faster polling DfRead to avoid dropping data.

However, this design has not yet specified the poll rate for DfRead. This design let the file be read on user demands, not upon events from File Size/State Monitoring sensor, and file data is not read regularly + stored in BMC, so it's likely not useful to handle chasing the file content updating rate.

Moreover, as point number 3. specifies, for SerialFIFO type, the design let pldmd call DfRead repeatedly until all the needed data is received, so I don't think DfHeartbeat is needed here.

I expect the implementation should have a subtle difference: The PLDM daemon will do reads from the host _while the client socket is writable_. If the client socket is not writable, then there may not be much point reading more data. If the system enters this state then yes, the PLDM daemon will only read data in response to the client socket becoming writable due to a client read. But otherwise, the PLDM daemon reads from the host are not directly instigated by a client read.

Essentially, the PLDM daemon is acting as a proxy. The client chooses whether it wants that data to hit persistent storage, be accumulated in memory, or streamed out e.g. the web interface. I think that's reasonable?
